label: M4 S4 | The Four Driver Frameworks — Formulas You Will Use for Every

formulas.name: Framework 1 — Store-Based (Retail)

variables.meaning: Total operational stores at the END of the forecast period (not opening). Forecast via: Opening Stores + Net Adds. Net Adds = Gross Adds − Closures.
Average annual revenue per store — serves as the base to which SSSG is applied. Note: this should be average across the base that existed in the prior year, not mixed.
Same-Store-Sales Growth — the year-on-year growth of stores that existed in BOTH years. Disclosed by most Indian retailers in investor presentations and concalls.

formulas.worked_example: Titan Jewellery FY25E forecast. FY24 Actual: 2,450 stores, Jewellery revenue ₹41,280 cr → Revenue per store ≈ ₹16.85 cr. Management guidance: 175 net store adds in FY25, with 8% SSSG. FY25E Store Count = 2,450 + 175 = 2,625. FY25E Revenue = 2,625 × 16.85 × 1.08 = ₹47,772 cr. Growth rate = 47,772/41,280 − 1 = 15.7%. Decomposing: store count growth contributes 7.1% (175/2,450), SSSG contributes 8.0%, slight mix effect contributes the rest. Any investor can challenge 'are you sure about 8% SSSG?' and you can respond with concall guidance or peer benchmarks. That is defensibility.
formulas.sensitivity_note: SSSG is the most investor-scrutinised driver in Indian retail. A 100 bps miss on SSSG (8% assumed vs 7% actual) directly reduces revenue by ~1% in that year. For companies where margins are sensitive to fixed-cost leverage (most retailers), a 1% revenue miss can translate to a 3-5% EBITDA miss. In Session 12's DCF, a persistent 100 bps SSSG cut can remove 8-12% from target price for retail names.

formulas.name: Framework 2 — Volume-Price (Manufacturing, Commodities, Autos)

variables.meaning: Physical units sold — cars, tonnes of steel, smartphones, etc. Forecasted via capacity × utilisation × sales efficiency.
Price per unit AFTER discounts, rebates, and returns. For companies with product mix, this is a weighted average — low-end ASP × share + high-end ASP × share.

formulas.worked_example: Maruti Suzuki FY25E forecast. FY24 Actual: 2.14 million units sold, average realisation ₹5.25 lakh/unit, revenue ₹1,12,430 cr. Management guidance: 8% volume growth (export push + domestic SUV expansion), 2% realisation growth (mix shift toward Brezza/Grand Vitara + price hike pass-through). FY25E Volume = 2.14 × 1.08 = 2.31 million units. FY25E Realisation = 5.25 × 1.02 = ₹5.36 lakh. FY25E Revenue = 2.31 × 5.36 × 10^5/10^7 = ₹1,23,720 cr. Growth = 10.0% (1.08 × 1.02 = 1.1016). Now I can argue: 'I'm forecasting 8% volume based on Suzuki's Manesar capacity expansion coming online Q2 FY25, plus the Kharkhoda plant adding 250,000 units annualised. Realisation growth of 2% reflects a 300 bps shift in mix toward SUVs, which have 18% higher ASP than compacts.' That is a concrete forecast.
formulas.sensitivity_note: For cyclicals (autos, metals, cement), realisation is often the dominant driver. A 5% price hike drops straight to the top line with no additional cost — a pure margin gain. Understanding whether a revenue forecast is volume-led or price-led is critical because price-led revenue growth often compresses margins on the next cycle turn. Always decompose and communicate the split.

formulas.name: Framework 3 — Unit Economics (Internet, Platforms, Fintech)

variables.meaning: Monthly Transacting Users — users who placed at least one paid transaction in the month. Sometimes disclosed as MAU (Monthly Active Users) — MTU is a stricter, more monetisable definition.
Frequency of ordering — how many orders an average MTU places per month. Drives engagement economics.
The average spend per order in rupees. Includes mix of delivery fees, discounts netted, service fees.
The percentage of Gross Order Value (GOV) that the platform keeps as revenue. For food delivery typically 20-25%; for quick commerce higher; for marketplace lower.

formulas.worked_example: Zomato Food Delivery FY25E. FY24 Actual: 18.5 million MTUs, 3.7 orders/MTU/month, ₹430 AOV, 21% take rate. GOV = 18.5 × 3.7 × 12 × 430 / 10^4 = ₹35,305 cr. Revenue = 35,305 × 21% = ₹7,414 cr. FY25E assumptions: MTU grows 12% to 20.7 million (disciplined customer acquisition), Orders/MTU flat at 3.7 (engagement mature), AOV grows 5% to ₹451 (menu premiumisation), Take Rate expands to 22% (platform fee scaling). FY25E Revenue = 20.7 × 3.7 × 12 × 451 × 22% / 10^4 = ₹9,110 cr. Growth of 22.9% — but now I can defend each component: MTU growth is disciplined, AOV growth is premiumisation, take rate expansion reflects platform fee strategy.
formulas.sensitivity_note: The Unit Economics framework is extremely powerful because it reveals which driver is the 'LEVER' vs which is saturating. For mature internet businesses, MTU growth is typically slowing (single-digit) but AOV and take rate still have runway. Distinguishing 'growth from volume' from 'growth from monetisation' is how PMs assess sustainability. Zomato bulls argue take rate has 400 bps more room; bears argue MTU saturation kills the flywheel.

formulas.name: Framework 4 — Utilisation-Billing (IT Services, Professional Services)

variables.meaning: Billable headcount (excludes support, admin, bench). For IT services, disclosed as 'software professionals' or 'delivery headcount.'
Percentage of billable hours actually billed. For Indian IT majors typically 82-87%. Key operational metric.
Realised rate per billable hour, after discounts. Driven by onsite/offshore mix, digital mix, and geographical mix.
Standard working hours per year — typically 2,080 (52 weeks × 40 hours) minus leave/holidays, so effective ~2,000.

formulas.worked_example: Infosys FY25E. FY24 Actual: 317,000 employees (of which ~250,000 billable), 83.5% utilisation, ~$32.50 effective billing rate, revenue $18.6 bn. Check: 250,000 × 83.5% × 32.5 × 2000 = $13.6 bn — but this is on a pure hourly basis; Infosys also has fixed-price projects that distort the pure formula. In practice, the framework is: Headcount × Revenue per Employee. FY24 Revenue per employee = $18.6 bn / 317K = $58,700. FY25E: Headcount growth slows to 3% (317K → 327K), but revenue per employee grows 4% (pricing + vertical mix shift). FY25E Revenue = 327K × $58,700 × 1.04 / 10^9 = $20.0 bn. Implied growth: 7.5%. Defensibility: 'I'm assuming modest headcount growth because hiring has slowed industry-wide; revenue per employee growth of 4% reflects improved utilisation (~100 bps) plus digital mix improving realisation.'
formulas.sensitivity_note: For IT services, the pure utilisation-billing framework often breaks down because of fixed-price deals and managed services. A simpler and more common framework is 'Revenue per Employee × Headcount.' Revenue per Employee is the composite KPI that captures utilisation, billing rate, and mix — all in one number. Track it over 5 years and forecast its trajectory — that's Motilal Oswal's, Kotak's, and Nomura's standard approach for IT coverage.

formulas.name: Framework 1 — Store-Based (Retail)

variables.meaning: Total operational stores at the END of the forecast period (not opening). Forecast via: Opening Stores + Net Adds. Net Adds = Gross Adds − Closures.
Average annual revenue per store — serves as the base to which SSSG is applied. Note: this should be average across the base that existed in the prior year, not mixed.
Same-Store-Sales Growth — the year-on-year growth of stores that existed in BOTH years. Disclosed by most Indian retailers in investor presentations and concalls.

formulas.plain_english: This formula decomposes retail revenue growth into two independent drivers: store count expansion and sales growth from existing stores. It tells you that a retailer's top-line trajectory depends on both footprint expansion (how many stores) and same-store performance (how much each store sells). For investors, it forces clarity: is growth coming from opening new markets, or from customers buying more at existing locations? If SSSG is falling, store expansion may be masking underlying weakness.

worked_example.problem: Forecast Titan Jewellery FY25E revenue using the store-based framework.
steps: FY24 Actual baseline: 2,450 stores, Jewellery revenue ₹41,280 cr → Revenue per store = 41,280 / 2,450 ≈ ₹16.85 cr
Management guidance: 175 net store adds in FY25, with 8% SSSG disclosed in concall
Decompose growth: store count contributes (175/2,450) = 7.1%; SSSG contributes 8.0%; interaction effect = 0.6% → 15.7% total
worked_example.result: FY25E Jewellery revenue ₹47,772 cr, representing 15.7% YoY growth
worked_example.insight: By decomposing, you can challenge each driver independently. A peer or analyst might ask 'are you sure about 8% SSSG?' — you respond with concall guidance or peer benchmarks (e.g., Asian Paints typically runs 6-9% SSSG in core painted segments). This defensibility is critical in live meetings. Also note: a 100 bps miss on SSSG (7% vs 8% assumed) reduces FY25E revenue by ~1.3%, which for margin-sensitive retailers can trigger a 3-5% EBITDA miss if fixed costs don't flex.

formulas.sensitivity_note: SSSG is the most investor-scrutinised driver in Indian retail. A 100 bps miss on SSSG (8% assumed vs 7% actual) directly reduces revenue by ~1% in that year. For companies where margins are sensitive to fixed-cost leverage (most retailers), a 1% revenue miss can translate to a 3-5% EBITDA miss. In Session 12's DCF, a persistent 100 bps SSSG cut can remove 8-12% from target price for retail names.

formulas.name: Framework 2 — Volume-Price (Manufacturing, Commodities, Autos)

variables.meaning: Physical units sold — cars, tonnes of steel, smartphones, etc. Forecasted via capacity × utilisation × sales efficiency.
Price per unit AFTER discounts, rebates, and returns. For companies with product mix, this is a weighted average — low-end ASP × share + high-end ASP × share.

formulas.plain_english: This framework isolates volume (how many units) from price (revenue per unit), revealing the true economic drivers. Many companies report revenue growth that masks deteriorating unit economics — volume may be flat or declining while rising prices temporarily inflate the top line. By separating volume and price, you can identify whether growth is sustainable (volume-driven, market-share gains) or cyclical (price-driven, likely to reverse). Essential for valuing cyclical businesses.
computation: Step 1: Gather FY24 actual revenue and total units sold to calculate baseline Average_Realisation_per_Unit = Revenue / Volume_Units
Step 2: Forecast FY25 Volume_Units using company guidance, capacity commentary, or peer benchmarks
Step 3: Forecast Average_Realisation_per_Unit growth separately — consider product mix shifts, price hike pass-through, and discount trends
Step 4: Multiply: FY25E Revenue = FY25E Volume × FY25E Average_Realisation

worked_example.problem: Forecast Maruti Suzuki FY25E revenue using the volume-price framework.
steps: FY24 Actual: 2.14 million units sold, revenue ₹1,12,430 cr → Average realisation = 112,430 / 2.14 = ₹52,542 per unit (or ₹5.25 lakh/unit)
Management guidance from concalls: 8% volume growth (export push + Kharkhoda plant expansion), 2% realisation growth (mix shift toward SUVs + price hike pass-through)
worked_example.result: FY25E revenue ₹1,23,720 cr, representing 10.0% YoY growth decomposed as 8.0% volume + 2.0% price
worked_example.insight: This decomposition allows you to defend the forecast in detail: 'Volume growth of 8% is supported by Kharkhoda plant adding 250,000 annualised units starting Q2 FY25, visible in management capex guidance. Realisation growth of 2% reflects three elements: (1) ~300 bps mix shift toward SUVs (Brezza, Grand Vitara have 18% higher ASP than compacts), (2) ~100 bps from passing through commodity/wage inflation, (3) −100 bps from higher discounting in the compact segment.' Now you can test sensitivity: if volumes miss by 100 bps (7% vs 8%), revenue misses by 1%; if realisation misses by 50 bps due to pricing pressure, revenue misses by 0.5% — manageable. But if both miss, downside is 1.5%, which could violate your analyst consensus.

formulas.sensitivity_note: For cyclicals (autos, metals, cement), realisation is often the dominant driver. A 5% price hike drops straight to the top line with no additional cost — a pure margin gain. Understanding whether a revenue forecast is volume-led or price-led is critical because price-led revenue growth often compresses margins on the next cycle turn. Always decompose and communicate the split.

formulas.name: Framework 3 — Unit Economics (Internet, Platforms, Fintech)

variables.meaning: Monthly Transacting Users — users who placed at least one paid transaction in the month. Sometimes disclosed as MAU (Monthly Active Users) — MTU is a stricter, more monetisable definition.
Frequency of ordering — how many orders an average MTU places per month. Drives engagement economics.
The average spend per order in rupees. Includes mix of delivery fees, discounts netted, service fees.
The percentage of Gross Order Value (GOV) that the platform keeps as revenue. For food delivery typically 20-25%; for quick commerce higher; for marketplace lower.

formulas.plain_english: This framework breaks platform revenue into four independent levers: how many users transact (user base), how often they transact (engagement), how much they spend per order (monetisation), and what slice the platform captures (take rate). It reveals whether growth is coming from acquiring new users (scalable but expensive), deepening engagement (sustainable), raising prices (risky), or expanding margins through take rate (operationally complex). For internet businesses, this decomposition is the foundation of investor credibility.
computation: Step 1: Calculate Gross Order Value (GOV) = MTU × Orders_per_MTU × 12 months × Average_Order_Value
Step 2: Multiply GOV by Take_Rate to derive Revenue
Step 3: Alternatively, forecast each component independently for different scenarios (e.g., disciplined MTU growth, stagnant frequency, premiumisation AOV)

worked_example.problem: Forecast Zomato Food Delivery FY25E revenue using unit economics.
steps: FY24 Actual baseline: 18.5 million MTUs, 3.7 orders/MTU/month, ₹430 AOV, 21% take rate
FY24 Revenue = 35,305 × 21% = ₹7,414 cr (verify against reported revenue)

FY25E assumptions: MTU growth 12% → 20.7 mn (disciplined CAC focus), Orders/MTU flat at 3.7 (engagement mature, per concall), AOV +5% → ₹451 (menu premiumisation, restaurant pricing power), Take Rate +100 bps → 22% (cloud kitchen fees, platform fee improvements)
worked_example.result: FY25E Food Delivery revenue ₹9,110 cr, representing 22.9% YoY growth
worked_example.insight: Now you can defend the forecast granularly: (1) MTU growth of 12% is disciplined — not chasing Tier 3 cities where unit economics are poor; based on Tier 1/2 expansion and same-city deepening. (2) Orders/MTU at 3.7 reflects mature platform saturation in cities like Bangalore/Mumbai; frequency unlikely to grow much. (3) AOV +5% is realistic — premiumisation of menu (more branded restaurants, higher check sizes), and management's ability to pass on delivery inflation. (4) Take rate +100 bps is credible — cloud kitchen fees recently introduced, platform fees trending up. However, bears will argue: 'If Orders/MTU is flat, how do you get 22% revenue growth?' You respond: 'It's come from three vectors: (1) bigger user base (12% MTU), (2) bigger spend per order (+5% AOV), (3) bigger cut per rupee (1% take rate expansion). None is extreme in isolation — but together they compound to 22%.' This is rigorous model accountability.

formulas.sensitivity_note: The Unit Economics framework is extremely powerful because it reveals which driver is the 'LEVER' vs which is saturating. For mature internet businesses, MTU growth is typically slowing (single-digit) but AOV and take rate still have runway. Distinguishing 'growth from volume' from 'growth from monetisation' is how PMs assess sustainability. Zomato bulls argue take rate has 400 bps more room; bears argue MTU saturation kills the flywheel.

formulas.name: Framework 4 — Utilisation-Billing (IT Services, Professional Services)

variables.meaning: Billable headcount (excludes support, admin, bench). For IT services, disclosed as 'software professionals' or 'delivery headcount.'
Percentage of billable hours actually billed. For Indian IT majors typically 82-87%. Key operational metric.
Realised rate per billable hour, after discounts. Driven by onsite/offshore mix, digital mix, and geographical mix.
Standard working hours per year — typically 2,080 (52 weeks × 40 hours) minus leave/holidays, so effective ~2,000.

formulas.plain_english: This framework models IT services revenue as a function of people, how much they're being utilised, and what rate clients will pay them. It reveals that IT services revenue is fundamentally a labour-arbitrage and skill-mix story: can you hire cheaper, bill higher, keep them busy, and shift them toward higher-margin work? The formula also exposes operational risk: if utilisation drops (bench builds up), revenue falls sharply even if headcount stays flat. This is why IT service investors focus heavily on utilisation and 'revenue per employee' as the composite KPI.
computation: Step 1: Gather FY24 actual revenue and calculate Revenue_per_Employee = Total Revenue / Total Employees
Step 2: Forecast Employees growth using company guidance (hiring plans, attrition rates, offshore expansion)
Step 3: Forecast Revenue_per_Employee growth separately — driven by utilisation improvement, billing rate hikes, and mix shift (digital, vertical specialisation)
Step 4: Multiply: FY25E Revenue = FY25E Employees × FY25E Revenue_per_Employee. This is simpler than the pure hourly formula because it bakes utilisation and rate into a single composite metric.

worked_example.problem: Forecast Infosys FY25E revenue using the utilisation-billing framework.
steps: FY24 Actual: 317,000 total employees (~250,000 billable), 83.5% utilisation, ~$32.50 effective billing rate (blended across geographies and verticals), revenue $18.6 bn

Note: pure hourly calculation (250K billable × 83.5% util × $32.50 rate × 2,000 hours) gives ~$13.6 bn, but Infosys has fixed-price projects that add ~$5 bn — this is why the revenue-per-employee shortcut is more reliable than the pure hourly decomposition

FY25E Assumptions: Headcount growth slows to 3% (317K → 327K, hiring discipline post-COVID), revenue per employee grows 4% ($58,700 → $61,048). Growth drivers: utilisation +100 bps (better project mix, less bench), billing rate +200 bps (digital services pricing power, onsite mix), vertical mix +100 bps (finance vertical premium pricing)
worked_example.result: FY25E revenue $20.0 bn, representing 7.5% YoY growth
worked_example.insight: By separating headcount growth (3%) from revenue-per-employee growth (4%), you communicate that Infosys is shifting from hiring-driven expansion to productivity-driven margin expansion. This is critical for valuation: a mature IT services company growing 7.5% on 3% headcount + 4% RPLE is fundamentally different from one growing 7.5% via headcount alone. Investors reward the former (efficiency, leverage) and penalise the latter (commoditisation risk, capex burden). In a live meeting, you'd say: 'I'm forecasting modest headcount growth because industry hiring has slowed, utilisation is already at 83.5%, and further bench compression is hard. Revenue per employee growth of 4% comes from (1) digital services mix (higher billing), (2) onsite deployment optimization (rate arbitrage), (3) vertical focus (finance commands 10% higher rates than infrastructure).' This shows granular understanding beyond a top-down growth rate.

formulas.sensitivity_note: For IT services, the pure utilisation-billing framework often breaks down because of fixed-price deals and managed services. A simpler and more common framework is 'Revenue per Employee × Headcount.' Revenue per Employee is the composite KPI that captures utilisation, billing rate, and mix — all in one number. Track it over 5 years and forecast its trajectory — that's Motilal Oswal's, Kotak's, and Nomura's standard approach for IT coverage.
